name: Monkey

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: An energetic music historian focused on the golden era of 1960s American dance crazes.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The monkey emerged as a novelty fad dance in the United States following the global breakthrough of the Twist in the late 1950s and early 1960s.
Wikidata dates the dance's inception to circa 1960, listing it as inspired by the Twist.
It reached its peak national popularity during the summer of 1963.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The monkey functioned as a lighthearted teenage novelty and fad dance, offering youth an accessible, entertaining way to participate in the burgeoning R&B and rock and roll dance craze boom of the early 1960s.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance was popularized by rhythm and blues and pop singles in 1963, notably Major Lance's 'The Monkey Time' and the Miracles' 'Mickey's Monkey'.
Both songs reached the pop Top 10 during the summer of 1963.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Major Lance and the Miracles were central to popularizing the dance through their 1963 hit records.
The Miracles' song 'Mickey's Monkey' credited the spread of the dance to William 'Mickey' Stevenson.
The monkey is an offshoot of the broader early-1960s dance craze wave initiated by the Twist, existing alongside peers like the Jerk, the Pony, the Watusi, the Mashed Potato, and the Funky Chicken.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Monkey is parent of Twist: The Twist inspired a wave of early 1960s fad dances, including the monkey.
Monkey is sibling of Jerk: A fellow 1960s novelty dance craze inspired by the success of the Twist.
Monkey is sibling of Mashed Potato: Another prominent fad dance of the early 1960s novelty dance boom.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.vocal_style: 1960s R&B vocal delivery with humorous storytelling lyrics
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Monkey (United States). Vocal style: 1960s R&B vocal delivery with humorous storytelling lyrics. Mood: novelty, upbeat, energetic, playful. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
